emails.reference_summary: This message was not from Fenwright Payroll; the sender's address and the link both use look-alike names that the real vendor does not own. Your direct deposit is fine, and you did the right thing by reporting instead of clicking.
emails.notes: The anchor email: the first body a student sends to a model in week 1, the first record a student parses into strict JSON in week 2, and one of the week 3 extractor cases. Key facts: the From domain fenwright-pay.example is a hyphen-insertion lookalike of the payroll vendor fenwrightpay.example, and the attacker owns it, so he publishes SPF and DKIM for it and collects spf=pass, dkim=pass and dmarc=pass; the lie is the domain and the display name, not the authentication, which is the single lesson this email exists to teach. The domain publishes a DMARC record with policy none, so policy.dmarc=none and dmarc_policy is none. The display name Fenwright Payroll Support carries the vendor name Fenwright Payroll, which display_names.json puts on fenwrightpay.example alone, so the week 3 display-name check reports sender:display_name_claims_vendor. The reputation record for fenwright-pay.example is status unknown, first seen 2026-04-13, one message in 90 days and no prior reports, so the domain is new. The one link host, my.fenwrightpay.example.secure-verify-login.example, is the subdomain trick: the real portal name my.fenwrightpay.example sits as three ordinary labels under the unrelated organizational domain secure-verify-login.example, so a reader who stops at the first familiar words is wrong, and check_urls returns unlisted. The path /account/login gives url:login_path. There is no Reply-To, no attachment and no In-Reply-To. The recipient is the service manager, an ordinary mailbox with no flags. Verdict malicious, category credential_phish. Difficulty reason: three decisive facts (the lookalike From domain, the display name claiming the payroll vendor, the subdomain trick in the link) and no pressure against them, so the base tier is easy; there is no injection and the body-only read agrees with the truth, so neither adjustment applies. Escalation: the rule table auto-contains an ordinary credential phish to an ordinary recipient with no interaction, so escalate_expected is false and the action is block_and_purge: block the URL host, purge copies, reply to the reporter. Loop reason: no single tool is decisive on its own, since check_sender_reputation returns unknown rather than known_bad and check_urls returns unlisted rather than blocklisted, so the bounded loop runs all three tools and ends with none left to try. Body content: the two urgency phrases are 'action required' and 'within 24 hours' and the two credential phrases are 'confirm your direct deposit' and 'sign in'; no payment, payment-change, payment-timing, data, gift-card, secrecy, file-share or account-change phrase appears, so the urgency and the credential ask are the only content indicators. The body is judgeable from its own text, which is what week 1 needs: the masthead and the signature both claim the payroll vendor, and the link is written out in full in the plain part, so a reader with no headers and no tools still sees the vendor name used as a label under a stranger's domain. Header tells: X-Priority: 1 with Importance: high, both stamped by the sender, which is header:x_priority_high; the gateway stamped X-Sentrywick-External: yes with scan result clean and spam score 2.9, so nothing in the gateway verdict argues against the message and a student who waits for the gateway to call it bad waits forever. There is no X-Originating-IP header: the sender is the attacker's own mail server rather than a webmail provider, and the manifest lists no header:x_originating_ip indicator, so the client address 192.0.2.151 appears in the bottom Received line instead. Rendering notes: the plain part is 7bit with hard wraps under 78 characters and the HTML part is quoted-printable, because the fixed gateway banner snippet is longer than 78 characters; the banner is the first line of the plain part and the first line after the body tag in the HTML part; both parts carry the same wording and the HTML part hides nothing, so there is no content:html_hidden_text. Line breaks in both parts are placed so that no content phrase is split across a line. Every identifier that looks random is derived from a SHA-256 over the corpus seed, the email id and a label, so the file regenerates byte for byte. The MIME boundary prefix is =_fwp_, the sender's own: =_swk_ belongs to the messages the Sentrywick stack composes, and this one was composed outside Pellgrave. Honest twin is 017.

emails.reference_summary: This is a real notice from our own help desk about Saturday's maintenance. Nothing needs to be done, and thank you for checking before clicking.
emails.notes: Key facts a correct extractor produces: from_domain pellgrave.example; reply_to_domain none (no Reply-To header); spf, dkim, dmarc and dmarc_policy all null, because the message never crossed the border gateway and the file carries no Authentication-Results header at all; display_name_mismatch false, since Pellgrave IT Help Desk is an owned name in data/display_names.json, owned by pellgrave.example and sourced from the shared mailbox helpdesk@pellgrave.example; url_hosts portal.pellgrave.example, from one link that appears once in the plain part and once in the HTML part, where the href and the visible text are the same address; no removed-attachment header; no In-Reply-To and no References, so the thread is new. Received chain: helpdesk-app.corp.pellgrave.example [10.20.8.15], the ticket system's submission host, handed the message to mail.pellgrave.example [10.20.4.25] with ESMTPSA at 08:15:01 -0500, and mail.pellgrave.example delivered it by LMTP to mailstore-01.pellgrave.example at 08:15:02; Date is 08:15:00. The list expanded at the submission host, so this file is the copy delivered to the reporter's own mailbox: the LMTP hop reads for <c.hallowden@pellgrave.example> and names mailstore-01, the store data/recipients.json gives that mailbox, while To stays all-staff@pellgrave.example, which is what recipient:distribution_list and the lookup_recipient expectation key on. recipients.json records mailstore-02 for the list itself, but the copy the corpus keeps is the one delivered to an individual member, so the LMTP hop names the reporter's own store, mailstore-01; every mailbox in the corpus lives on exactly one store whatever path a message took. Return-Path is <noreply@pellgrave.example> while From is helpdesk@pellgrave.example: the ticket system puts the envelope sender on its own mailbox, the one data/recipients.json records with worked_by null, so the delivery failures from several hundred list members go to a mailbox nobody works instead of the monitored shared help desk mailbox the notice is signed with. It is the same reason the message carries Auto-Submitted. The envelope sender is an RFC 5321 identity and the From mailbox is the RFC 5322 author, so the two differ on purpose, with no Sender header and no indicator: both addresses sit on pellgrave.example, which is the organizational domain sender:internal_domain keys on. X-Sentrywick-External is absent, which the extractor records as header:external_flag with the value no, and neither body part carries the gateway banner, because the gateway inserts it only into the mail it stamps as external. The gateway still wrote X-Sentrywick-Scan-Result: clean on its own submission, and X-Sentrywick-Reported-By names Casimir Hallowden, who reported it. The ticket system broadcasts this notice to a distribution list, so it also carries Auto-Submitted: auto-generated, the RFC 3834 section 5 header that keeps out-of-office replies from several hundred mailboxes out of the shared help desk mailbox; the extractor records it as header:auto_submitted. Body: multipart/alternative, a text/plain part then a text/html part, both 7bit and carrying the same words, so a part-to-part diff is empty; the HTML part is plain paragraphs with one anchor and no image, script, form, styling trick or hidden text. Content: the help desk announces that the intranet portal and the field service app go offline for planned maintenance on Saturday 4/18 from 6:00 to 9:00 AM, that both come back on their own and nothing is required of anyone, that portal.pellgrave.example serves only the status page while the window is open and the field app will not respond, that everything else keeps running and Saturday crews get their assignments from dispatch by phone as usual, that the status page at https://portal.pellgrave.example/status stays up through the window and shows where the work stands, and that anything still down after 9:00 goes to the help desk on ext. 4400 with a reference to ticket PMG-HD-20488. It signs with the shared mailbox name and extension 4400. The status page is carved out of the outage in the sentence that names the outage, so the one link in the message does not point at a host the message has just called unreachable, and the Saturday crews on phone dispatch keep a Saturday morning window credible at a contractor whose field technicians work Saturdays. Dispatch is an operations function and IT owns no dispatch extension, so the notice names no number for it and the help desk extension appears only in the closing line and the signature. Nothing in it asks for credentials, a payment, a payment date, data, secrecy or a reply on another channel; that extension is a contact route for a service that did not come back, not an offer to confirm a request by phone, so content:phone_verification_offered does not fire and no phrase from its list appears. The wording stays clear of every phrase list in spec/enums.json, which is why the window is named by its date and its clock times rather than by a countdown, why the field app will not respond rather than stop working, and why the record carries no content code. Difficulty reason: the tier rule counts one decisive benign fact, the organization's own domain on the internal path, against no pressure facts, so the base tier is easy; the body-only read is benign, the same as the verdict, so no adjustment applies. No injection. For the instructor: this is the week 1 contrast body. In week 1 the students send this body to the model with no extracted facts and no tools, and it has to read as ordinary internal housekeeping on its own words alone, against 001, the payroll deposit lure that is the other week 1 body. The forged copy of this help desk name is 006, which arrives in week 3, and its honest twin is 051 in the exam set; neither of those is in front of a student in week 1 or week 2. In week 2 the same body has to come back as strict JSON with verdict benign and category legit_internal. Full credit on the indicators criterion needs sender:internal_domain and url:host_internal_known_good, the two facts that separate this notice from an imitation of it: the sender is the organization's own domain arriving on the internal path, and the one link goes to a host on the internal known-good list in data/known_good_domains.json. The week 4 loop should stop after one call: check_sender_reputation returns status internal at domain level, which is the stated stop condition, so stop_reason is internal_sender; check_urls would only confirm that portal.pellgrave.example is internal, and lookup_recipient would only confirm that all-staff@pellgrave.example is a distribution list with no report history of its own. Escalation: none. The verdict is benign, the category is legit_internal, and no benign escalation rule fits, since nothing here fails authentication on a trusted sender, touches a banking item or asks an unknown sender's question, so recommended_action is close_benign_reply_to_reporter. Story context: Casimir Hallowden reports almost every message that carries a link, and his record shows 11 prior reports with 0 true positives, so a benign internal notice is exactly what his reports usually are. The queue needs that traffic: an agent that never sees a real help desk notice learns to treat the help desk name itself as the tell.

Week 4 use: check_sender_reputation matches inkmoor-office.example at the organizational-domain level even though the From host is news.inkmoor-office.example; check_urls returns unlisted for the tracking host, which playbook rule 7 reads as unknown, not clean; lookup_recipient shows the chronic reporter (11 reports, 0 true positives). The footer's postal line stops at a box number because the corpus names no city, state or postal code anywhere. emails.reference_summary: This did not come from Rutger; the address is on a look-alike domain that is not ours, and it pushes for a fast payment by email only. We are treating it as an attempted fraud, and no payment should be made.
emails.notes: Business email compromise with no link and no attachment: the fourth category week 2 needs, the display-name versus sender-domain case in week 3, and the week 5 loop path where calling check_urls is the wrong second move. Key facts: the display name Rutger Palomares is the company's real Chief Financial Officer, whose address is r.palomares@pellgrave.example, while the From domain is pellgrave-corp.example, an added-word lookalike the attacker registered and published SPF and DKIM for; no Reply-To; SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass for pellgrave-corp.example, which publishes a DMARC record with policy none, and that pass proves only that the mail came from the attacker's own domain; the message arrived through the gateway (X-Sentrywick-External: yes) with a clean scan and a spam score of 3.4; there is no link, no removed attachment and no In-Reply-To. Difficulty medium by the tier rule: two decisive facts (sender:display_name_matches_employee and sender:lookalike_domain) against one pressure point (no link and no attachment, so check_urls has nothing to check), which is decisive over pressure without a tie, and neither adjustment applies because there is no injection and the body-only read already lands on malicious. Playbook rule that decides the case: rule 2, an employee's name over an address outside pellgrave.example is impersonation until a phone call proves otherwise, which is also where the callback in the close comes from. Rule 5 is not cited and does not reach this message: it covers a change to a vendor's bank details or to when a payment goes out, and this is a first payment to a vendor with no details on file and no scheduled run, which is why the record carries content:payment_request and neither content:payment_change_request nor content:payment_timing_request. A student who cites rule 2 alone has the whole answer. Body signals: the ask is a same-day payment before a named meeting, the amount and the vendor are given, the remittance details are promised in a later message, and the sender rules out the phone and asks for email only, which is the pattern that keeps the real Rutger from being reached. The payee named in the body, Quillbeck Controls, appears in no other record and in none of data/sender_reputation.json, data/domain_policy.json, data/url_allowlist.json, data/url_blocklist.json or data/url_unlisted.json. It is a name with no domain, no address and no link behind it, so the body hands the loop nothing further to look up and no fourth fact hides outside the answer key; the Rookmere chiller project, which 008 and 054 also name, is likewise a project name with no domain in this body. That is deliberate: the whole week 5 lesson here is that the agent has nothing left to call. Corroborating context rather than a scored indicator: X-Mailer says Marrowdale Mail 5.2 and the bottom Received hop is client-04.pellgrave-corp.example [192.0.2.62] handing the message in over ESMTPSA, both the shape of a desktop client, while the body closes 'Sent from my phone' and uses the phone as the reason the sender cannot be called. An analyst should read that contradiction and a student who finds it is right, but the indicator vocabulary in spec/enums.json has no code for a mailer or hop that disagrees with the body, so nothing scores it; the phrase itself is already carried by content:channel_restriction. Tools: check_sender_reputation matches at domain level and returns status unknown with new_domain true and first_seen 2026-04-14, the day this message arrived; lookup_recipient shows Priya Castellanos is an ordinary mailbox that handles payments, with six reports and four true positives in 90 days; check_urls has nothing to look up, so the loop stops on tools_exhausted after two calls rather than spending a step on a tool with no input. That is the week 5 lesson this email carries. recipient:prior_similar_report is absent by the prior_similar_report_rule: content:payment_request is not an ask code, the message carries no payment change, timing or gift card ask, and the sender record has no campaign tag, so no tag is collected and no campaign ties this message to any other record. Expected action: escalate_incident for financial_or_endpoint_impact, because a malicious BEC always escalates whatever the recipient's flags say. Priya is not an executive, so executive_target does not apply, and she reported the message before acting on it, so user_interacted does not apply. The correct close is to confirm with Rutger at his extension, block pellgrave-corp.example, and tell accounts payable that no payment was set up.

emails.notes: Attacker-owned added-word lookalike of the electronic signature vendor. larkseal-docs.example publishes its own SPF record (mx -all), signs with selector k1 and publishes a DMARC record with policy none, so spf, dkim and dmarc all pass for the domain the message names. The passes prove only that the attacker owns larkseal-docs.example, which is why auth:all_pass counts for nothing in the tier rule. The display name Larkseal claims the vendor whose real domain is larkseal.example, and the notice imitates that vendor's signing request so the CEO appears to have sent her own assistant a customer contract. Key facts: from_domain larkseal-docs.example; reply_to none; spf pass; dkim pass; dmarc pass (policy none); url_hosts larkseal-docs.example, one link that appears once in each body part; no attachment; no In-Reply-To. Playbook rules 2 and 7: a vendor's name over a domain the vendor does not own is impersonation, and a blocklisted link host is malicious. Difficulty easy: four decisive malicious facts (sender:lookalike_domain, sender:display_name_claims_vendor, sender:known_bad, url:host_blocklisted), no pressure toward benign, no injection, and no body-only reversal. The three content codes are recorded because the phrase lists in spec/enums.json match the rendered body ('sent you a document', 'expires in', 'sign in'), and all three carry polarity PB, which the tier rule counts only for a benign verdict, so they leave the count at decisive 4 and pressure 0. No url:login_path: the only link is https://larkseal-docs.example/sign/request/<reference> with the anchor text 'Review document', where 'sign' is the electronic signature verb and neither the path nor the link text asks anyone to log in. The sign-in ask lives in the prose and is carried by content:credential_request. body_only_read is uncertain because the body alone is an ordinary signing notice: it names a real customer agreement and asks for nothing but a click, so nothing in the prose decides the case and every decisive fact comes from a tool or a header. Week 5 loop: check_sender_reputation returns known_bad at domain level, first seen 2026-03-12, two prior reports, last report malicious on 2026-03-19, campaign tag fake-esign-share, which is decisive on the first call, so the loop stops after one step with stop_reason decisive_malicious. A loop that goes on to check_urls learns the same thing from the blocklist and spends a step for nothing, which is the shortest path in the week 5 set and the contrast case for 012, where no tool is decisive and the run hits the cap of 4.
